body.hook: Every note in Western music, all twelve of them, is in the chromatic scale. Once you can play it cleanly, there's no note in your range you can't reach. That's why advanced players treat the chromatic scale as a daily workout.

study.title: The Twelve-Note Workout
study.question: How do I practise technique efficiently?
study.passage:
The chromatic scale moves in half steps. From concert B♭ up an octave: B♭ B C C♯ D E♭ E F F♯ G A♭ A B♭.
Sharps are usually used going up and flats going down, but they are enharmonic (the same pitch).
Part 1, Learn it in chunks (15 minutes): Split the octave into three chunks of four notes. Play each chunk slowly with a metronome at 60, two notes per beat. Check fingerings or slide positions on your chart, including alternate fingerings (for example, chromatic F♯ fingering on flute or the side B♭ on saxophone).
Part 2, Practice strategy (10 minutes):
1. Slow: play at a tempo where you make no mistakes.
2. Repeat correctly three times in a row.
3. Raise the metronome by 4 beats per minute.
4. If you make a mistake, go back down.
Part 3, Full scale (10 minutes): Play the full octave up and down, then extend to your range.
Part 4, Practice log: Record your starting and ending tempo and the trickiest note change.

body.hook: Every band piece has that one run of fast notes that makes players nervous. Professionals don't just play it over and over at full speed; they take it apart, fix the exact problem and rebuild it.

study.title: Taming Fast Passages
study.question: How do I fix a difficult technical passage?
study.passage:
Technical passage toolkit (written for this lesson):
1. Diagnose: play the passage once slowly. Circle the exact two or three notes where it breaks (often a hard finger change or register crossing).
2. Isolate the problem notes: play just the two notes back and forth 10 times smoothly.
3. Chunk: split the run into groups of 4 notes; play each group, pausing on the first note of the next group ("stop on the beat").
4. Rhythm variations: play even sixteenths as long-short (dotted), then short-long. This trains each finger move.
5. Backward chaining: play the last group, then the last two groups, and so on to the beginning.
6. Tempo ladder: start at a tempo you can play 3 times perfectly; raise by 4 BPM; if you make a mistake, drop back 8.
7. Finger efficiency: watch in a mirror; keep fingers low and relaxed.
Apply to one passage from the concert music; log start and end tempo.

study.title: Practise Smarter
study.question: How do I make my practice time count?
study.passage:
The 30-minute practice plan (written for this lesson):
1. Warm-up (5 minutes): long tones with tuner; lip slurs or register exercises.
2. Technique (8 minutes): scales or chromatic scale with metronome; one articulation pattern.
3. Repertoire focus (12 minutes): one or two tricky spots using the technical toolkit; set a measurable goal ("Bars 33–36 at 100 BPM, 3 times clean").
4. Run-through (3 minutes): play a whole section without stopping, as in performance.
5. Reflect (2 minutes): write what improved and the goal for tomorrow.
Feedback tools: metronome (tempo), tuner (pitch), phone recording (tone, rhythm, dynamics; listen back with the music).
Science of practice: spreading practice across several days (spaced practice) generally works better than one long cram session. Short breaks help focus.
Activity: plan a week of practice in your journal, record yourself on day 1 and day 5, and compare.
